items.title: DJI’s New SDR Transmission 2 is Set to Bring Stronger Interference Resistance and Better Image Quality
items.summary: It’s hard to cover DJI's new product announcements without making the whole story about the fact that another helpful, kind of cool piece of film and video gear is set to be released everywhere in the world except the United States. But here we are. The DJI drone ban that has now expanded pretty much into an everything ban continues on, and another new DJI product has been revealed, with the DJI SDR Transmission 2 looking like a nice follow-up to the company’s previous model, but it, sadly, does not look like it’s set to be available in the US anytime soon. The DJI SDR Transmission 2 A follow-up to the original DJI SDR Transmission, which actually is available in the US as a complete wireless video transmission kit, this new version is set to provide stronger interference resistance, better image quality, and greater range. The DJI SDR 2 will work in the most crowded sets, maintaining a high-bitrate, low-latency feed even in complex environments with lots of competing signals. The DJI SDR Transmission 2 will include a TX/RX switchable transceiver design and will be Ronin series compatible, aiming to bring pro-grade performance to a compact, lightweight form factor. Price and Availability The DJI SDR Transmission 2 will be available for purchase directly from DJI or authorized dealers, but only outside the US. If you live outside the US, or are just curious, here are the full specs and a purchase link to the DJI site (which likely won’t load if you’re in the US). 1 TX to 8 RX With Control, Multi-Group Transmission Auto Channel 2.0 for Seamless, Stable Feed TX/RX Switchable for Flexible Deployment Pairing-Free Connection for Fast Camera Switching Supports Ronin Monitoring & Control DCI 4K/60fps 10-bit HDR Wireless Transmission Price: Roughly $400 for the base unit.

items.title: Portkeys Has a New LH5P III On-Camera Monitor With a Rugged, But Lightweight, Design
items.summary: Another new on-camera monitor option is on the market, and we couldn’t be happier. These are the golden days of production monitors, as there are truly a billion to choose from, with pretty much all of them being great, versatile, and affordable. If you’re in the market for a new on-camera monitor, or looking for more options to build out your gear closet, the new Portkeys LH5P III is another solid option with plenty of versatility, daylight-viewable brightness, and a uniquely durable yet lightweight design. Here’s what you need to know. The New Portkeys LH5P III Designed to be compact, rugged, and lightweight at the same time, the new Portkeys LH5P III is another 5.7-inch on-camera monitor with wired and wireless camera control. The Portkeys LH5P III is an HDMI-only monitor that should work on any set or in any setting, as it is fully daylight-viewable with a maximum brightness of 2,200 nits. The monitor also covers 104% P3 Color Gamut Area Ratio, and the display is Calman-calibrated with a DeltaE ≤ 1.1 in Rec.709 and a DeltaE ≤ 2.5 in P3. As mentioned above, one of the more unique factors here is that the monitor will weigh only 235g/8.29oz (making it 18% lighter than its predecessor) and will feature a thickness of just 28.4mm/1.1in, making it about as slim and lightweight as any on-camera monitor option on the market, yet still durable and capable for most filmmaking and video needs. Price and Availability The Portkeys LH5P III is out and available now and is powered by the company’s MOVNORM OS, and is set to come with pretty much everything you’d need to start working with it right away. Here are the full specs and purchase links to the company’s website. 5.7-inch panel with a resolution of 2160 x 1080 and a 1400:1 contrast ratio. Daylight-viewable with a maximum brightness of 2,200nits. 10-bit hardware processing with 104% P3 Color Gamut Area Ratio Factory Calman color-calibrated: DeltaE ≤ 1.1 in Rec.709 and DeltaE ≤ 2.5 in DCI-P3. 1 x HDMI input, 1 x HDMI out

items.title: Is Steven Spielberg’s ‘Munich’ the Best Directed Movie Ever?
items.summary: The best channel on all of YouTube for film essays is Patrick (H) Willems, whose dissections of movies and TV are must-watch for anyone trying to understand media. I legitimately think they are better than many college courses on the topic, and I think Patrick is a hero both in his quest for understanding and in media literacy. Even when I don't always agree with his videos, I learn something I never knew. And it actually has opened me up to a deeper understanding not just of other people's work, but in trying to channel my own voice as well. So when I tell you, Patrick has made what could be his best video of all time, I hope you listen. It's a dissection of Steven Spielberg's Munich, and it's this beautiful look at who Spielberg is as a person and hiw work in front of and behind the camera. It posits that Munich is the best-directed movie ever, and I walked away agreeing. In his video essay, Willems breaks down not just why Munich is Spielberg’s most underrated film, but also why it is a masterclass in visual storytelling, economy of coverage, and formal control — the likes maybe we've never seen before or since. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The 21st-Century "Jazz Period" In order to understand Spielberg's work on Munich, you first have to look at the movies that came before it. Yes, that's a lot of films, so we're just going to focus on the immediate movies before it that sort of shaped Spielberg's worldview. Patrick affectionately called it Spielberg's "Jazz period," but I also like to think of it as his immediate pre- and post 9/11 persiod where he was trying to figure out what the hell was going on in the world. items.title: How the NFL and Hallmark Invented A Rom-Com Playbook
items.summary: My wife and I are football fans. I am a member of Eagles Nation, and she's born and bred with the Vikings. It divides our house, except when we come together to watch on Sunday mornings, as long as we're not playing each other. The NFL has the strongest fanbase of any professional sport, and it proudly says that its fanbase is roughly 50% women. Now, these women are into the sport and into watching it, but as they try to expand its reach, they also want content outside the game that appeals to women. Enter The Hallmark Channel, a place my wife turns every Christmas to watch all of these cheesy, sweet movies about people getting together. You could say that Hallmark is the NFL of romantic comedies, at least in terms of its market share. Well, in a recent report by The Ankler, the partnership between Hallmark, the NFL, and Skydance Sports is proving that scripted genre entertainment might be the future of these kinds of partnerships. Let's dive in. The Plug-and-Play Scripted Formula Okay, so if you have seen the NFL Hallmark movies, or any Hallmk movies, you know these are a little formulaic. They are what we'd call a comfort watch for many, designed not only to bring in the team's fans but also to bring in women who maybe aren't into football, and to approach them in their own world. The blueprint is as follows... Pick an NFL franchise. Set a feel-good romantic comedy in its home city. Cameo active players and team legends as exaggerated versions of themselves. The next part is getting couples, or just women, to sit down and enjoy that and then engage with football, too. items.title: Movie Lines Presidents and Politicians Have Borrowed
items.summary: You probably love to quote films as much as I do. It's fun to reference what our favorite characters say, almost like a code among savvy cinema fans. The lines that last often do so because of their impact or rhetorical value. Sometimes the best way to say something is in another character's voice, with the skill and word choice of an orator, so we can crib those lines to express ourselves in the same way. Sometimes a line can enter daily life so thoroughly that it just becomes standard. I can forget sometimes that politicians are sometimes just as nerdy as the rest of us. When they hear a really good line of dialogue, it can end up in the mouth of a sitting president, a governor, or another candidate, sometimes as a deliberate borrow, sometimes as a hot-mic accident. These lines can end up shaping policy fights, campaign messaging, and other speeches. Here are five examples and the lines that became political tools. - YouTube www.youtube.com Reagan and Dirty Harry On March 13, 1985, President Ronald Reagan was at a White House briefing for the American Business Conference. The Senate Budget Committee had been talking about tax increases. Reagan borrows Harry Callahan's line from Sudden Impact (written by Joseph Stinson, with the "make my day" phrase widely attributed to John Milius). He turned it into a veto threat. "No matter how well-intentioned they might be, no matter what their illusions might be, I have my veto pen drawn and ready for any tax increase that Congress might even think of sending up," he said, per UPI. "And I have only one thing to say to the tax increasers: 'Go ahead—make my day.'" He liked the line. A lot. Three years later, Reagan referenced the moment when addressing the same group. items.title: Apple Reveals Its New AirPods 5, But Are They Ready for Editing and Production Work?
items.summary: In the true spirit of DIY filmmaking, the brand or type of headphones that you use for production or editing matters about as much as your cameras, lenses, or any other parts of the process. If you have a good story, clear vision, and great actors, you’re liable to find success regardless of your gear. Yet, with that being said, there are plenty of gear decisions that can make your life easier, and many decisions that can make things harder on yourself. Choosing the right headphones when you need them is one of those decisions, and while Apple AirPods have been getting more popular, they still haven’t been considered for production or video-editing needs. Could that change with Apple's new 5th-generation AirPods? Let’s take a look. Apple AirPods 5 Revealed Revealed by Apple at its "Surprise and Shine” event, this newest generation of the AirPods promises some nice improvements in a few key areas. The first is noise cancellation, as the AirPods 5 will feature 1.5x more active noise cancellation than previous models. The AirPods 5 will also offer enhanced Siri functionality and an open-ear design for all-day comfort, which could help with production or editing work in particular. The new AirPods will also provide personalized spatial audio with head tracking and be more immersive than ever with impressive new Live Translation upgrades that let wearers communicate across 10 languages. Ready for Video Work? Keeping the point above in mind about how any gear could work for the right DIY creators, of course, some high-quality headphones from a tech-forward company like Apple are going to be capable of getting the job done. They should be more comfortable and, if you work in immersive video, the immersive audio features should be a plus. Still, with so many extremely comfortable over-ear headphones on the market from brands that specialize in sound and video editing, AirPods likely won’t be your best bet for long sessions. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The Ryan Gosling Quote That Made the Driver an Instant Icon
items.summary: When Drive came out, it was like the only soundtrack I saw people buying on vinyl. Everyone was obsessed with this synth neo-noir that thrust Ryan Gosling back into the spotlight and showed everyone he was a star. There's this energy when you watch this movie still. It's so tight and edited so precisely; every scene and every movement feel like they matter, because it's all about someone driving and motoring the narrative forward. Gosling's nameless lead character, known simply as "The Driver," is a man of few words, but the ones he does say count and reveal what he believes and who he is from the opening of the movie. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Scene in Question The quote I want to go over from Drive is almost the opening lines of the movie. And for writers, here's something I think you can zone in on. You want to give your character a code. Something we know they believe. Well, this movie does that in spades. And then it gives us a scenario where that code either must be upheld or broken. The film opens in a dimly lit, run-down apartment. The Driver sits on the edge of the bed, holding a phone to his ear, staring blankly ahead. His voice is monotone. He's laying out his terms of service. "There's a hundred-thousand streets in this city. You don't need to know the route. You give me a time and a place, I give you a five minute window. Anything happens in that five minutes and I'm yours. No matter what. Anything happens a minute on either side on that and you're on your own. Do you understand?" - YouTubewww.youtube.com What The Quote Means What makes this line so brilliant from a screenwriting perspective is how much work it does in under ten seconds to set up the story and reveal who this character is right away. items.title: VOR-Bench: A Human Perception-Driven Benchmark for Video Object Removal
items.summary: arXiv:2609.16878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite its crucial role in video object removal (VOR), existing evaluation paradigms face two critical limitations: questionable references and a misalignment between tradi- tional metrics and human preference. To address these challenges, we introduce VOR- Bench, which advances VOR evaluation through three integrated components. First, we present the VOR Dataset (VORD), the first benchmark dataset providing both paired edited videos and graffiti masks. Its unique strength lies in a diverse data spectrum, which encompasses model-generated, tool-rendered, and camera-captured data, ensuring robust assessment across real-world scenarios. Second, we develop rMPAF, a realistic Motion- capable Paired-video Acquisition Framework. By combining the strengths of image- based object removal and fine-tuned video generation models, rMPAF automatically generates realistic, motion-coherent paired videos. Finally, we propose three evaluation dimensions and introduce VOR-MDSM, the first perception-driven VLM-based scoring model specifically designed for mask-guided VOR. It bridges the gap between arithmetic metrics and human perception by covering the essential visual attributes and matching nuanced human judgment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VOR-Bench yields evaluation results that align closely with human perception, achieving a remarkable cor- relation (\r{ho} > 0.9) with subjective assessments. We will release VOR-Bench along with its documentation to ensure full reproducibility.

items.title: FROD: Feature Matching Residual Denoising Oracle Bone Decipher
items.summary: arXiv:2609.17227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Oracle bone script (OBS), one of the earliest Chinese writing systems, plays an important role in the study of Chinese etymology. Traditional decipherment relies heavily on domain experts who analyze characters through semantic context and structural evolution. To assist this labor-intensive process, we formulate OBS decipherment assistance as a cross-era image translation task and propose FROD (Feature Matching Residual Denoising Oracle Bone Decipher). Although many OBS characters differ substantially from their modern counterparts, they often preserve local topological invariants at the radical level. During training, FROD leverages fast feature matching to provide gated segmentation supervision: paired samples with sufficient matches are processed patch-wise to align fine-grained radicals, whereas low-similarity pairs are trained holistically to avoid mismatched artifacts. In addition, a Residual Denoising Diffusion Model (RDDM) jointly estimates noise and residual signals, thereby reducing the positional drift and stroke disorder commonly observed in standard diffusion models. Finally, a multi-stage font stylization refinement network refines the generated images by eliminating edge noise and stabilizing stroke structures. On our augmented character-disjoint dataset, FROD achieves higher Top-1 recognition accuracy than the evaluated baselines, with a 3.8% absolute gain over OBSD.

items.title: 4 Lessons on Building a Storytelling Life
items.summary: How do you find your creative voice? Actually, what is a creative voice? Simply put, your creative voice is how your perspective and experiences shape the way you tell stories. Your background will lead you to notice details, visually or in behavior or in sounds, that others won't. If you grew up, say, in a place where drought was prevalent, your attitude toward water would likely differ from someone who grew up in a rainy climate. Each would photograph water differently, or have characters treat it differently. We want to look at this topic today with the help of Bill McDonald. He has been head of cinematography at UCLA's School of Theater, Film and Television since 1998 (formerly, he served as Department of Film, TV and Digital Media chair and is an ASC Associate Member). He has spent decades helping new filmmakers figure out what kind of storytellers they are. He sat down with the ease podcast at UCLA's Sound Stage 3 for a wide-ranging conversation about voice, curiosity, and the physical and psychological demands of a creative life. Let's learn the big takeaways in the video below. - YouTube www.youtube.com Voice Starts with a Question One thing that filmmakers often get stuck on is aesthetics. And it's understandable why, because filmmaking is a visual medium, and they want things to be "pretty" or "interesting" or "cool." They want to copy a cool shot they saw one time for the heck of it because it seems like the thing they should do. If you're doing that, you're probably in the process of finding your voice and tone. McDonald says that the wrong metric is aesthetic, and the right one is the question you keep coming back to. "What are the stories, what are the characters, what are the human actions that you're interested in? You just endlessly explore." He brought up family dynamics as a topic he constantly comes back to, because he grew up in a large family. This doesn't mean that you find a voice and have to stick to it forever.
